scenes.title: The Binomial Theorem
scenes.promise: Expand any power of a bracket — and pick out one term without expanding at all.

scenes.heading: Why expanding by hand dies
scenes.text:
Expanding $(1+x)^2$ by hand is fine. $(1+x)^3$ — still fine.

By $(1+x)^5$ you are multiplying five brackets and collecting six terms. One slip anywhere wrecks the lot.

This topic gives you a formula that writes any of these down in one line — and grabs any single term on its own.

scenes.heading: The same curve, one power higher each time
scenes.caption: Each power of $(1+x)$ is still just a polynomial. Watch the coefficients: $1,1$ → $1,2,1$ → $1,3,3,1$ → $1,4,6,4,1$ — each row is the previous row's neighbours added together (Pascal's triangle).

scenes.heading: The numbers in front
scenes.text:
Those coefficients — $1, 4, 6, 4, 1$ — are the **binomial coefficients**, written $\binom{n}{r}$ and read "$n$ choose $r$".

You never work them out by hand: press $^nC_r$ on your calculator. $\binom{7}{2}$ is 7 $\,^nC_r\,$ 2 $\,= 21$.

scenes.heading: The binomial theorem — it's on your formula sheet

callouts.label: $a$'s power falls, $b$'s rises — in every term the two powers add to $n$

scenes.heading: The workhorse: the general term
scenes.intro: One formula grabs any term on its own — also on the formula sheet:

callouts.label: the $(r+1)$th term — $r=3$ gives the 4th term, not the 3rd
second term's power rises: $r$ — its sign stays inside

steps.note: Match the formula: $a=2$, $b=3x$, $n=5$. The whole of $3x$ is $b$ — the 3 rides inside the power.
The $x$'s only come from $(3x)^r$, so the power of $x$ is $r$.
Substitute $r=3$ everywhere — and $T_{3+1}$ is the 4th term.
Coefficient of $x^3$: $\,1080$. No full expansion anywhere.

scenes.heading: When a bracket sits in front
scenes.text:
Exams love $(k+2x)(\ldots)^6$. Don't expand everything.

Each part of the front bracket picks out whichever term of the expansion lands on the power you want. Want $x^3$ overall? Then $k$ needs the bracket's $x^3$ term, and $2x$ needs the bracket's $x^2$ term.

Expand only as far as you need — then collect.

scenes.prompt: Your turn — a real O-Level question (GCE 2023). Use the general term on the bracket, then pair each part of $(k+2x)$ with the right term.
scenes.why: $k$ pairs with the bracket's $x^3$ term and $2x$ pairs with its $x^2$ term: $-20k + 2(60) = 0$, so $k = 6$.

scenes.heading: The other classic: the term independent of x
scenes.intro: "Independent of $x$" means the power of $x$ is ZERO. Find that term in $\left(x^2 + \frac{2}{x}\right)^{\!6}$.

steps.note: The habit that earns the marks: (numbers) × (powers of $x$). $\frac{1}{x^r} = x^{-r}$.
Multiplying powers of $x$: ADD the exponents. $12 - 2r - r = 12 - 3r$.
Set the power to zero and solve. $r$ must land on a whole number — if it doesn't, the term does not exist.

scenes.heading: The slip that costs the most marks
scenes.text:
When the bracket is $(a-bx)^n$, the minus lives INSIDE $b$.

$(-2x)^3 = -8x^3$ — the power hits the coefficient AND the sign AND the $x$. Odd $r$ keeps the minus; even $r$ kills it.

Write the second term in brackets, with its sign, every single time.

scenes.prompt: Last one. "No term in $x^2$" means that coefficient equals zero — and keep the minus inside $\left(-\frac{a}{3}x\right)^{\!r}$ while you work.
scenes.why: Pairing up for $x^2$: $\;3 \times \frac{80a^2}{3} + 5 \times (-64a) = 80a^2 - 320a = 0$, so the positive constant is $a = 4$.

scenes.heading: You own the workhorse now
scenes.text:
General term → one power of $x$ → set the power to what you want → solve for $r$ → substitute back.

That is the whole topic. Every exam variation is this loop with different scenery — go make it automatic.
